item.title: Awake intubation in a Japanese tertiary emergency department: a single-center retrospective descriptive study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Evidence on awake intubation in emergency departments (EDs) is limited. We aimed to describe patient characteristics, intubation indications, procedural practices, and outcomes for awake intubation in the ED.

Methods: This single-center retrospective descriptive study included consecutive adult patients who underwent tracheal intubation at a tertiary ED in Japan from April 2020 through December 2025. Patients intubated during cardiac arrest were excluded. Operational definition for awake tracheal intubation required topical upper airway anesthesia, no neuromuscular blockers before or during the initial attempt, and documented preservation of consciousness and spontaneous ventilation throughout that attempt. Outcomes included first-pass success, adverse events related to airway management, and definitive airway management, including rescue.

Results: Eighty-four patients underwent awake tracheal intubation, representing 5.5% of intubations in patients without cardiac arrest (84/1531). Upper airway infectious diseases were present in 54 patients (64.3%); airway-related indications accounted for 63 cases (75.0%). Emergency physicians performed 79 initial attempts (94.0%); a flexible bronchoscope was used initially in 49 patients (58.3%). First-pass success occurred in 63 patients (75.0%; 95% confidence interval, 64.4%-83.8%). Seven patients (8.3%) experienced adverse events related to airway management. Eighty patients (95.2%) achieved definitive airway management without a surgical airway. Four patients (4.8%) required a surgical airway, all after first-pass failure.

Conclusions: Awake intubation, performed primarily by emergency physicians, was used to manage upper airway infectious diseases with actual or impending obstruction in a tertiary ED. A flexible bronchoscope was used initially in over half of cases and most patients were intubated without a surgical airway.

item.title: One-year mortality following emergency department visits for stimulant toxicity
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Objective: Rising stimulant-related overdose deaths and emergency department (ED) utilization highlight the need to better characterize outcomes following ED encounters for stimulant toxicity. We sought to determine one-year mortality after ED discharge for stimulant toxicity and to characterize the causes of death.

Methods: This retrospective cohort study used a linked statewide database of ED and hospital discharge records and death records. Patients discharged from the ED with a primary diagnosis of stimulant toxicity, identified by International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes, were included. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality within one year of ED discharge, estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis. A secondary reference analysis was performed among patients with ED visits for acute opioid toxicity to contextualize mortality estimates against a population previously associated with elevated post-discharge mortality.

Results: A total of 2356 patients met inclusion criteria. One-year mortality was 2.1% (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.6-2.8%). Among patients who died within one year, median age at the index visit was 35 years and median time to death was 118 days (interquartile range [IQR] 63-228 days). Overdose accounted for 67% of deaths, with opioids implicated in 54% and combined opioid-stimulant involvement in 37%. In the secondary reference cohort of 1665 opioid-related ED visits, one-year mortality was 6.9% (95% CI 5.8-8.3%).

Conclusion: Patients with ED encounters for stimulant toxicity experienced substantial one-year mortality in a relatively young population. Subsequent deaths were predominantly overdose-related and frequently opioid-involved, supporting consideration of opioid-focused harm-reduction interventions in this population.

item.title: Disparities in investigation of physical abuse among trauma patients
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Physical abuse is a significant public health issue in the United States, leading to poor health outcomes such as chronic illness, depression, and substance abuse. Research regarding how the medical system addresses physical abuse in the overall adult population is scarce. The objective of this study was to assess disparities in investigation of physical abuse among adult trauma patients.

Methods: This is a retrospective analysis of the 2017-2019 American College of Surgeons-Trauma Quality Program database. This study included all adult patients (≥18 years) who had a report of physical abuse by the medical team to authorities. Chi square and multivariate analysis were applied where appropriate to assess which characteristics showed disparities in investigation rate.

Results: On univariate analysis, there were disparities with regard to age, mechanism, race, ethnicity, payment method, and mental health or substance use disorder. On multivariate analysis, male sex, non-penetrating trauma, age ≥70, American Indian race, and presence of a mental health disorder were associated with decreased odds of investigation. Non-elderly adult patients made up a disproportionate amount of abuse victims.

Conclusions: This study shows significant disparities in the escalation of a physical abuse report to an official investigation in the trauma setting. The authors recommend increased advocacy and resource allocation for these vulnerable populations in the clinical setting as well as further research regarding to what extent patient choice versus discretion of authorities influences these disparities. The authors also recommend a larger research focus on non-elderly adult victims of abuse.

item.title: Tongue capillary refill time and imaging parameters for acute coronary syndrome identification: A prospective ED study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Rapid identification of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in emergency department (ED) patients with chest pain remains challenging. Tongue capillary refill time (CRT) and tongue imaging may reflect systemic perfusion, but their value in ACS is unknown.

Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of standardized tongue-derived perfusion, macroscopic, and imaging parameters for identifying ACS.

Methods: This prospective observational study enrolled 208 consecutive adult ED patients presenting with chest pain. Standardized tongue imaging and tongue CRT were assessed. A separate 20-patient pilot assessed interobserver reliability using ICC and kappa coefficients. Blinded ACS adjudication used clinical findings, serial high-sensitivity troponin measurements, electrocardiography, imaging studies, specialist consultations, and follow-up data. ROC analysis and multivariable logistic regression were performed.

Results: Among 208 patients, 61 (29.3%) had ACS: 16 STEMI, 41 NSTEMI, and four unstable angina cases. Tongue CRT was significantly prolonged in ACS patients (2.6 [2.2-2.9] vs. 1.3 [1.1-1.6] seconds; p<0.001). Tongue CRT demonstrated excellent discrimination for ACS (AUC 0.941, 95% CI 0.903-0.980), outperforming the HEART score (0.860), admission troponin (0.831), and TIMI score (0.788). A CRT threshold ≥2s yielded 86.9% sensitivity and 93.2% specificity. Tongue CRT and macroscopically dry tongue remained associated with ACS after adjustment (both p<0.001). Quantitative RGB and HSV parameters showed no significant between-group differences.

Conclusions: Standardized tongue CRT showed excellent discrimination for ACS in this cohort, in which most ACS cases were myocardial infarction. Its diagnostic value in unstable angina and incremental clinical utility remain unestablished. External validation is required before routine clinical use.

item.title: An original closed reduction technique for acute shoulder dislocation: The FEAT method
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Purpose: The objective of this study was to introduce a novel closed reduction technique, termed the FEAT (Fixation, External rotation, Alignment, Traction) method, for anterior shoulder dislocations and to evaluate its effectiveness, speed, reliability, and safety.

Methods: This prospective study enrolled 30 patients presenting with anterior glenohumeral dislocation at the Emergency or Orthopedics outpatient department of Hubei Provincial Hospital. Closed reduction was performed using the FEAT method without administering analgesics, muscle relaxants, or anesthetics. Only a single reduction attempt was permitted per patient. The time required for successful reduction was recorded, and patient-reported pain intensity during the procedure was assessed using a visual analog scale (VAS) ranging from 0 to 10.

Results: All 30 patients experienced successful reduction on the first attempt. The average time required for successful reduction was 54.3 s, with a mean VAS pain score of 3.67 during the procedure.

Conclusion: The FEAT method is an effective, rapid, and minimally painful technique for anterior shoulder dislocation reduction. Its simplicity and ease of mastery support its widespread clinical adoption.

item.title: Latent class phenotypes and emergency department disposition for patients with traumatic subdural hematoma and midline shift
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Guidelines recommend surgical evacuation for traumatic subdural hematoma (SDH) with >5 mm midline shift (MLS), but emergency department (ED) triage varies between the operating room (OR) and the intensive care unit (ICU). We investigated whether ED disposition to the OR versus ICU was associated with differences in outcomes and whether distinct patient phenotypes modified these associations.

Methods: We retrospectively identified adult patients from the ACS TQIP dataset with traumatic SDH, MLS >5 mm, and ED disposition to either the ICU or OR. We defined patient phenotypes using latent class analysis (LCA) and investigated associations between ED disposition and outcomes (inpatient mortality, favorable discharge) using risk-adjusted hierarchical logistic regression. We tested for interaction between patient phenotype and ED disposition and repeated these analyses among patients undergoing an ICU stay ≥1 day and cranial surgery.

Results: Among 9582 patients, 29% (N = 2794) were triaged to the OR. Two LCA-informed phenotypes emerged: class 1 (older-mild injury) and class 2 (younger-severe injury). There was an interaction between ED disposition and patient phenotype, such that younger-severe patients had lower mortality with OR triage (P < 0.001). In the subgroup of 4573 patients (48%) with ≥1 day of ICU stay who underwent cranial surgery, there was a significant interaction between OR triage and the older-mild phenotype indicating increased mortality (P = 0.003).

Conclusions: For traumatic SDH with MLS >5 mm, triage the OR was associated with improved outcomes only among younger, severely-injured patients, while older, mildly-injured patients may benefit from early ICU stabilization. These findings support phenotype-guided ED triage strategies to optimize outcomes.

item.title: Association between transfer pathways and functional outcomes in severe trauma patients: a cohort study using the PATOS registry
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Objective: Optimal transport strategies for severe trauma remain debated, particularly in Asia. We evaluated the association between interhospital transfer and functional outcome and its consistency across Asian trauma systems.

Methods: This cohort study used the Pan-Asian Trauma Outcome Study (PATOS) registry. We analyzed patients with severe trauma (Injury Severity Score > 15) in South Korea, Malaysia, and Vietnam (2015-2022). The exposure was interhospital transfer (Transfer) versus direct transport to a definitive-care hospital (Direct). The primary outcome was a favorable functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale ≤3). The primary model was a country fixed-effect logistic regression estimating the total effect; country-specific estimates and a transport-pathway × country interaction were pre-specified.

Results: Of 9857 patients (Direct, n = 6725; Transfer, n = 3132; 89.2% of transfers in South Korea), a favorable functional outcome occurred in 4701/6403 (73.4%) versus 1830/2991 (61.2%). Transfer was associated with lower odds overall (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.86, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.78-0.95), but estimates differed by country (South Korea 1.06, 0.95-1.18; Malaysia 0.53, 0.36-0.80; Vietnam 0.17, 0.11-0.25; interaction P < 0.001; I2 = 97.4%).

Conclusion: Interhospital transfer was associated with a lower likelihood of a favorable functional outcome, but this was not uniform across the three trauma systems and was dominated by Korean data, in which no association was observed. These findings require confirmation in analyses anchored at injury or first medical contact.

item.title: Injury patterns and early operative demand in a combined military and civilian casualty cohort: A single-centre study from the first 11 weeks of the 2023 Israel-Hamas war
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Modern asymmetric warfare and large-scale terror attacks produce distinctive wounding patterns that differ from conventional state-on-state conflict and impose specific early demands on receiving trauma systems. The 7 October 2023 attack on southern Israel and the ensuing war generated a compressed surge of combined civilian and military casualties. We characterized injury patterns and linked them to early in-hospital resource use at a single tertiary trauma centre across the opening weeks of the conflict.

Methods: We performed a retrospective descriptive cohort study of 192 consecutive trauma casualties admitted between 7 October and 24 December 2023. Demographics, mechanism of injury, injured anatomical regions, Injury Severity Score (ISS) and acute interventions were abstracted from the institutional trauma dataset. Mechanism and anatomical categories were not mutually exclusive. Variables were summarised as medians (IQR) or counts (percentages); missing data were not imputed and percentages were computed over non-missing observations.

Results: Casualties were young (median age 24 years, IQR 21-35) and predominantly male (84.4%). Penetrating (43.2%) and shrapnel (31.2%) mechanisms predominated, followed by acoustic trauma (12.0%). Extremities were most often injured (lower limb 41.7%, upper limb 35.4%); 68.8% had at least one extremity injury and 37.0% had two or more injured regions. Median ISS was 9 (IQR 4-16); 26.5% of those with a recorded ISS had ISS ≥16. Blast and crush carried the highest median ISS (25 and 16). Early resource use was substantial: 23.4% required emergency surgery via direct emergency-room-to-operating-room transfer, 10.9% mechanical ventilation and 5.2% packed red-cell transfusion.

Conclusions: This extremity-predominant, penetrating-and-shrapnel profile, with a small but disproportionately severe blast and crush subgroup and frequent acoustic trauma, translated into early demand for emergency surgery, ventilation and transfusion. These patterns support resourcing limb-salvage and damage-control surgery, blood-bank and intensive-care readiness, and audiologic follow-up in military and mass-casualty trauma planning.

item.title: Subcutaneous insulin for mild-to-moderate diabetic ketoacidosis: a scoping review and implementation framework
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Purpose: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a common emergency department (ED) presentation associated with high morbidity, mortality, and healthcare utilization. While intravenous (IV) insulin remains the most common treatment, emerging data suggest subcutaneous (SUBQ) insulin may be a feasible alternative for patients with mild-to-moderate DKA. This scoping review summarizes current evidence of SUBQ insulin use across a broad range of clinical and operational outcomes in DKA and provides an implementation framework for SUBQ insulin for mild-to-moderate DKA in the ED.

Methods: We conducted a scoping review of PubMed from inception through February 2026 for adult studies evaluating SUBQ insulin for DKA. Two investigators independently screened studies, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Data were charted and synthesized across clinical, operational, and implementation outcomes.

Results: A total of 117 articles were identified and 13 included. Available evidence suggests SUBQ insulin may achieve similar time to DKA resolution, compared with IV insulin in select patients with uncomplicated DKA. SUBQ insulin offers potential operational benefits, including reduced intensive care unit (ICU) utilization, shorter ED length of stay, and improved resource optimization. Patient selection criteria, dosing and monitoring strategies, and implementation approaches are summarized. Limitations in the literature include small sample sizes, single-center designs, heterogeneous protocols, and the exclusion of several higher-risk patient populations.

Conclusions: Evidence suggests SUBQ insulin pathways achieve similar clinical outcomes and may reduce ICU utilization and improve operational efficiency in select patients with mild-to-moderate DKA. Because most evidence originates from small, single-center cohorts, future studies should focus on larger, more generalizable populations.

item.title: Prehospital factors associated with calcium derangements upon arrival to the trauma center from scene - A subanalysis of a multicenter prospective study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Existing data suggests that hypocalcemia may be a factor in the lethal diamond of trauma. This could offer a potential opportunity for prehospital interventions to address these derangements. We performed a preplanned secondary analysis of data from a prospective multicenter study on calcium derangements in hemorrhage patients upon arrival at trauma centers.

Methods: We conducted a prospective multicenter observational study of trauma patients admitted at the highest level of activation for three participating centers where an ionized calcium level was measured upon arrival. Data from the prehospital records were collected from the Emergency Medical Services reports. We compared study variables between patients who were hypocalcemic, eucalcemic, and hypercalcemic.

Results: There were 1270 participants enrolled in our primary study, of whom 1047 arrived by EMS from the scene meeting inclusion for this analysis. Of these, 235 were hypocalcemic and 39 were hypercalcemic upon arrival. Patients with calcium derangements had lower survival compared to patients without derangements. Of those who were hypocalcemic, 32.8% received prehospital blood products, compared to 25.6% of those who were hypercalcemic upon arrival. There were 5 (12.8%) who were hypercalcemic that received prehospital calcium, potentially indicating iatrogenic hypercalcemia. Elevated prehospital shock indices were associated with both derangements. Of the 718 who received no fluids or blood, 116 (16.1%) were hypocalcemic and 27 (3.7%) were hypocalcemic with 2 hypercalcemic participants receiving calcium. Of those 136 that received a blood product prehospital, 77 were hypocalcemic (56.6%) with 1 receiving calcium, and 10 (7.4%) were hypercalcemic with 3 receiving calcium, and the remaining were eucalcemic with 4 (2.9%) receiving calcium.

Conclusions: Both hypocalcemia and hypercalcemia occurred in the setting of blood product and no blood product administration. Our study suggests that currently available assessment methods are inadequate for predicting the presence of a calcium derangement, both high and low.

item.title: Magnesium sulfate therapy for adult emergency department patients with acute asthma: A narrative review
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) has been used for decades as an adjunctive bronchodilator in acute asthma exacerbations refractory to first-line therapy, but its role in adult emergency department (ED) care remains debated.

Objective: To review the evidence for intravenous (IV) and nebulized MgSO4 as adjunctive therapy in adults presenting to the ED with acute asthma, to clarify how the pooled analyses and the largest individual trial relate to one another, and to compare this evidence with current guideline recommendations.

Methods: This is a structured narrative review. Records were identified from a PubMed search using a single search phrase (19 records), supplemented by targeted Cochrane Library and guideline-body searches performed in August 2026 (14 records) and by backward citation searching. Screening and data extraction were performed by a single reviewer. After removing duplicates and one record excluded for population mismatch, 29 records were assessed for eligibility. Ten provided extractable magnesium-specific efficacy or safety data, 5 primary randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and 5 systematic reviews or meta-analyses, which are presented separately because the reviews pool overlapping trials. The remaining 19 records were used only as background. Eighteen additional eligible RCTs included in these reviews were not identified by our search; these are listed, and their contribution is represented only through the pooled estimates of the reviews that include them.

Results: In pooled analysis, IV MgSO4 was associated with a modest reduction in hospital admission (Cochrane 2014, 11 trials including the 3 Mg trial: OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.60-0.92; number needed to treat approximately 14) and some short-term improvement in lung function. The largest individual trial (3 Mg, n = 1109), which contributes to that pooled estimate, found a similar but non-significant reduction in admission with IV MgSO4 (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.51-1.04), no benefit from nebulized MgSO4, and more adverse events with active treatment than with placebo (15.6% vs 10.1%; OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.11-2.52), most of which were minor. A larger lung-function benefit at the lowest baseline FEV1 was supported by one trial's prespecified interaction analysis, but a larger reduction in admission in the most severely obstructed patients rests on a small subgroup and was not confirmed by a test for subgroup differences across trials. A 2023 adult-specific meta-analysis found no statistically significant pooled lung-function benefit by either route. Commonly reported adverse effects were flushing, fatigue, nausea, headache, and transient hypotension.

Conclusion: IV MgSO4 may provide a modest benefit in selected adults with severe asthma exacerbations that do not respond to initial therapy. A greater benefit in the most severely obstructed patients is plausible but has not been established. Nebulized MgSO4 has no convincing evidence of benefit in adults. Major guidelines (GINA 2026, BTS/SIGN 158 [2019], and NAEPP EPR-3 [2007]) support IV MgSO4 as a second-line adjunct for severe or life-threatening exacerbations unresponsive to initial therapy, and GINA has not recommended nebulized MgSO4 since its 2025 update. Clinicians using IV MgSO4 in severe refractory asthma should expect a modest and uncertain benefit and an excess of minor, but rarely serious, adverse events.

item.title: Stroke mimics in the emergency department: Prevalence, etiologies, and clinical predictors in patients with suspected acute stroke
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Stroke mimics present with acute neurological symptoms resembling stroke and remain a major diagnostic challenge in the emergency department (ED). Early differentiation from true stroke is important for timely treatment and appropriate resource utilization.

Objective: To determine the prevalence, etiologies, and clinical predictors of stroke mimics among patients presenting to the ED with suspected acute stroke within 9 h of symptom onset.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults who presented to the ED of Srinagarind Hospital, Thailand, between January 2021 and December 2024. Eligible patients were aged ≥18 years, had suspected acute stroke within 9 h of symptom onset, and were triaged through the institutional Stroke Fast-Track protocol. Demographic characteristics, comorbidities, presenting symptoms, physical examination findings, and neuroimaging results were extracted from electronic medical records. Attending neurologists determined the final diagnoses. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses identified factors independently associated with stroke mimics.

Results: Among 1615 patients, 347 (21.5%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 19.5-23.5%) were diagnosed with stroke mimics. Seizure-related disorders were the most common etiology (13.8%), followed by cardiovascular and cerebrovascular non-stroke conditions (11.2%) and infectious or inflammatory diseases (10.1%). In multivariable analysis, younger age, male sex, a history of migraine, psychiatric disorders, and epilepsy, along with lower diastolic blood pressure and higher heart rate, were independently associated with stroke mimics. Presenting features independently associated with stroke mimics included altered consciousness (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.71; 95% CI, 1.25-2.33), seizure (aOR 2.68; 95% CI, 1.79-4.00), vertigo (aOR 1.85; 95% CI, 1.28-2.65), and fever (aOR 3.10; 95% CI, 1.36-7.12). Conversely, limb weakness and speech disturbance were independently associated with confirmed stroke.

Conclusion: Stroke mimics accounted for 21.5% of suspected acute stroke presentations in the ED. Altered consciousness, seizure, vertigo, and fever were independently associated with stroke mimics, whereas limb weakness and speech disturbance favored confirmed stroke.

item.title: Implementation of regional interfacility transfer guidelines for patients with isolated facial trauma: A preliminary report
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Objective: Secondary overtriage (SO) of isolated craniomaxillofacial (CMF) fractures overwhelm trauma centers and represent a significant resource burden while ultimately delaying patient care. The objective of this study was to implement an interfacility transfer protocol at a tertiary level 1 trauma center and review the preliminary utilization findings.

Methods: A tertiary academic medical center adopted the protocol via the AgileMD pathway in regional referral centers. The protocol indicates the necessity of on-call specialist consultation based on a patient's clinical presentation. This study conducted a retrospective cohort analysis for patients with isolated CMF trauma and AgileMD pathway activation over a one year period. The main outcome was transfer center activation.

Results: The pathway was utilized 55 times for isolated CMF trauma patients in one year. The majority of traumas involved nasal bone fractures (52.7%) and were most often caused by falls (49.1%). On-call specialist consultation occurred 18.2% of the time - down from 100% of cases prior to guideline institution. The majority of patients (78.2%) were discharged with 40.9% follow-up, while 16.4% were transferred. These dispositions followed the guidelines 90.9% of the time.

Conclusions: This is the first pilot study on the implementation of isolated CMF trauma interfacility transfer guidelines. The 81.8% reduction in on-call specialist consultation suggests a meaningful call burden reduction for surgical providers, while a discharge rate of 78.2% and outpatient follow-up rate consistent with pre-implementation levels reflects significant preservation of trauma resources. Broader adoption of similar protocols can further reduce SO, hospital costs, and wait times.
